feed.title: Yokohama & Fujisawa, Actually
feed.subtitle: Two cities south of Tokyo, written up by someone who lives here. Prices checked, trains timed.

entry.title: Enoshima's winter lights start on 1 December: dates, hours and prices
entry.summary: Shonan no Hoseki 2026-27 on Enoshima runs 1 December to 28 February. Lighting hours by date, entry prices after 17:00, and trains from Fujisawa Station.
entry.content:
Enoshima’s winter illumination, Shonan no Hoseki (湘南の宝石), starts on Tuesday 1 December 2026 and runs to Sunday 28 February 2027. Last season it opened on 22 November. If you planned a late-November evening around an older guide, the lights will be off.

The short version: the lights come on at 17:00. The main display is inside a garden at the top of the island, which costs ¥500 from 17:00. Going up the tower in the middle of it is listed as a further ¥800. From Fujisawa Station the train takes 7 minutes and costs ¥170, and then you walk for about 20 minutes.

This piece is desk research. Nobody visited for it. The dates, hours and prices come from three Japanese event listings that carry the organiser’s announcement, and they agree with each other.

The dates, and why older pages are wrong

This is the 27th edition. It was recognised in 2025 as one of Japan’s three great illuminations, which is why it turns up in most winter lists for the Tokyo area.

English lists can be a season behind. One English listing checked for this piece still gives the start as late November. Last season that was right: 22 November 2025 to 28 February 2026. This season the first night is 1 December, nine days later.

The lights are in three places: Enoshima Samuel Cocking Garden (江の島サムエル・コッキング苑) at the top of the island, other spots on the island, and the Katase coast on the mainland side. The listings name two fees, both inside the garden. They do not say whether the island and coast displays cost anything, so that is not stated here either.

Lighting hours change four times

On an ordinary weekday the lights run from 17:00 to 20:00. On Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays they run to 21:00.

From Saturday 19 December to Wednesday 30 December they run to 21:00 every night, weekdays included.

From Thursday 31 December to Sunday 3 January they stop at 20:00 every night, even on the weekend.

From Saturday 16 January the start moves to 17:30, for weekdays and weekends alike.

The listings for this season give no last-entry time. Last season it was 30 minutes before the lights went off: 19:30 on weekdays and 20:30 on weekends. Plan as if that still applies.

What it costs

There are two fees.

Entry to the garden is free until 17:00. From 17:00 it is ¥500 for adults and ¥250 for children.

The Sea Candle is the lighthouse tower inside the garden. Its fee is listed as ¥800 for adults and ¥400 for children. Its viewing floor is 41 metres above the ground and 101 metres above the sea.

The listings show these as two fees for two things. If both are charged in full, an adult who enters the garden and goes up the tower pays ¥1,300. No combined ticket price was confirmed for this piece.

Whether someone who walks into the garden at 16:50 is asked to pay at 17:00 was not confirmed either. Do not build your evening on that.

The train from Fujisawa Station is cheap. The Odakyu Enoshima Line to Katase-Enoshima (片瀬江ノ島) is ¥170 each way, ¥167 with an IC card. So the evening from Fujisawa Station comes to:

Adult
Odakyu, Fujisawa to Katase-Enoshima and back ¥340
Garden entry from 17:00 ¥500
Without the tower ¥840
Sea Candle ¥800
With the tower ¥1,640

Getting there from Fujisawa Station and from Yokohama

Fujisawa Station (藤沢) is the place to change. From Yokohama Station it is 20 minutes on the JR Tokaido Line. From Shonandai it is 7 minutes by Odakyu express and ¥200.

At Fujisawa you choose between two trains.

The Odakyu Enoshima Line takes 7 minutes to Katase-Enoshima and costs ¥170. Katase-Enoshima is the closest station to the island: about 20 minutes on foot to the garden.

The Enoden takes about 10 minutes to Enoshima Station (江ノ島) and costs ¥220. From there the walk to the garden is about 25 minutes. The two stations are 11 minutes apart on foot.

The Shonan Monorail’s Shonan-Enoshima Station is a third way in, about 26 minutes on foot from the garden.

For this trip the Odakyu line is ¥50 cheaper each way and leaves you five minutes closer. Take the Enoden if the Enoden itself is part of what you came for.

Train times and fares above are from route searches. The Fujisawa to Katase-Enoshima fares come from searches dated July to September 2026, and the others from 19 November 2026.

What is not good

It is a 20-minute walk before you see the main display, and it ends in a climb. The tower’s viewing floor is 101 metres above the sea and 41 metres above the ground, which puts the garden about 60 metres up.

On a weekday you have three hours, 17:00 to 20:00. From Shinjuku, the routes checked took between 62 and 112 minutes to Katase-Enoshima. Leave Tokyo after work and a large part of the three hours goes on trains.

The organiser extends the hours every night from 19 to 30 December. That is a fair sign of when the most people are expected. If you can choose, the first two and a half weeks of December and the weeks after mid-January are the other options, and from 16 January you lose the first half hour.

It is an island, in winter, after dark. Nothing in the listings says what happens in bad weather.

The organiser’s own page could not be opened when this piece was checked. Before you travel, confirm the hours and fees on the official Shonan no Hoseki page (Japanese).

If you only remember three things

The first night is 1 December.

Bring ¥500 for the garden, and ¥800 more if you want the tower.

From Fujisawa Station, take the Odakyu line to Katase-Enoshima.

entry.title: The map residents actually use for Yokohama and Fujisawa
entry.summary: A resident's orientation to Yokohama and Fujisawa: population by ward, the three railways linking them, and fares and times checked in November 2026.
entry.content:
Most guides give you two dots. One is Yokohama’s harbour: Minato Mirai, Chinatown, Yamashita Park. The other is Enoshima, the small island off Fujisawa’s beach. Both are worth a day. Together they cover a thin slice of the two cities.

I live in the rest. My home is in Izumi ward, a part of Yokohama I call its countryside. I’m a software engineer and a father of two, and I ride a 125cc Honda Monkey. This site is where I write the two cities down as the people here use them, with the prices and the minutes checked.

This first piece is the map. Learn three railway lines and everything else on the site will fall into place.

Yokohama is 18 wards, and the harbour is two of them

Yokohama had 3,753,462 residents on 1 October 2026, by the city’s own estimate. It is the most populous municipality in Japan. Tokyo is larger, but Tokyo is run as 23 separate wards, each counted on its own.

The city covers 438 square kilometres and is divided into 18 wards (ku, 区). The harbour that visitors photograph sits in two of them, Nishi and Naka. On 1 November 2024 those two wards held about 261,000 people, out of 3.77 million. That is about 7%.

The other 93% live inland and along the railways. Kohoku ward alone had 365,668 residents in July 2026. Most visitors never hear the names of wards like Totsuka, Asahi, Izumi and Seya, and that is where a large part of the city sleeps.

This has a practical consequence. The Yokohama of supermarkets, schools, rents and commutes is the inland one. If you are choosing where to stay for a week or where to live for a year, the harbour tells you little.

Fujisawa is three towns stacked north to south

Fujisawa is smaller: about 445,000 people on the resident register on 1 January 2025. It has been a city since 1940. Enoshima is part of it, which surprises people who assume the island belongs to Kamakura next door.

Think of Fujisawa as three bands.

The south is the coast on Sagami Bay: the beaches of Katase, Kugenuma and Tsujido, and Enoshima. The land here is flat.

The middle is Fujisawa Station (藤沢), where the shops are, and where JR, the Odakyu line and the Enoden meet.

The north is low hills, and its main station is Shonandai (湘南台). Three railways stop there, and two of them end there.

Six railway operators run inside this one city: JR’s Tokaido Main Line, Odakyu, Sotetsu, the Enoden, the Yokohama Municipal Subway and the Shonan Monorail. That much track is the reason Fujisawa works as a base for a whole trip, well beyond one afternoon on the island.

Three lines tie the two cities together

The JR Tokaido Line is the fast one. Fujisawa Station to Yokohama Station takes 20 minutes. Stay inside the JR gates, ride the Negishi Line one more stop, and you are at Sakuragicho (桜木町), the station for the harbour. The JR fare from Fujisawa to Sakuragicho is ¥440.

The Blue Line is Yokohama’s municipal subway. It has 32 stations and runs from Azamino in the north of the city to Shonandai. Its last stop is across the city boundary, in Fujisawa. From Shonandai it reaches Sakuragicho with no change in 37 minutes for ¥370. It is slower than JR, and you never have to think.

The Sotetsu Izumino Line also ends at Shonandai. It reaches Yokohama Station by way of Futamatagawa (二俣川). On the trains checked for this piece, the ride was 11 minutes to Futamatagawa and 16 minutes on from there, and the fare for the whole ride was ¥370.

Inside Fujisawa, the Odakyu Enoshima Line joins the north to the middle. Shonandai to Fujisawa Station is 7 minutes by express and costs ¥200. The same line continues to Katase-Enoshima, the station nearest the island. The Enoden leaves from Fujisawa Station too, and runs along the coast to Kamakura.

Every fare and time above is for a weekday morning, looked up on 19 November 2026. With an IC card such as Suica or PASMO a few of these fares come out ¥1 to ¥7 lower.

Old guides have the wrong JR fares

JR East raised its fares on 14 March 2026. The company described it as its first fare revision since it was created in 1987, and the minimum fare went from ¥150 to ¥160. A JR fare printed in a guide from before that date is wrong.

Every fare on this site carries the date it was checked. When a fare changes, the piece gets corrected and the correction is dated.

What is not good about this map

The lines do not meet where you want them to. Shonandai and Fujisawa Station are both in Fujisawa, and they are 7 minutes and ¥200 apart on a different company’s train.

Japanese railways charge per operator. A trip that uses two companies costs two fares. Shonandai to Sakuragicho is ¥370 on the Blue Line alone. Go by Odakyu and JR through Fujisawa Station and the same trip is ¥640. It took 43 minutes on the morning checked, 6 minutes longer than the subway. The route that looks clever costs ¥270 more and saves no time.

The Blue Line is slow. Those 37 minutes cover 20.4 km, which works out to about 33 km/h.

And this map leaves out buses, which many inland neighbourhoods depend on. No bus fares were checked for this piece, so there are none in it.

How to use it

If you are visiting, choose where you sleep by line. A hotel near Yokohama Station is 20 minutes from Fujisawa Station on JR, and Fujisawa Station is where the Odakyu line and the Enoden leave for Enoshima.

If you are thinking of living here, choose the line first and the ward second. The line decides your commute and your fare. The ward decides which city office you queue at.

Before you compare two routes, count the companies. One company, one fare.

Every piece on this site says which line it is on.
